As of 240 AM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall 
is expected tonight through Friday, with a few thunderstorms 
possible.

Early morning surface analysis shows the area of high pressure 
offshore with a cold front approaching the western edge of the 
state. There is a band of light showers on radar moving through 
central VA as of this writing. A brief couple of hundredths of 
an inch of rain will be possible if you're under one. Light 
scattered showers will remain possible through just after 
daybreak. Additionally, guidance shows some patchy fog 
potentially developing across the southern VA Piedmont down into
interior NE NC between 5-8am, though it shouldn't be nearly as 
widespread or dense as it was yesterday morning. 

Another warm day is anticipated today as southerly flow 
increases ahead of the approaching front. High temperatures are 
forecast to climb into the mid to upper 70s, with a few 
locations across SE VA and NE NC approaching 80 degrees. Skies 
will remain mostly cloudy, and a few isolated showers will be 
possible throughout the afternoon. However, the more widespread 
rainfall is expected to hold off until Thursday night. 

The front will reach our CWA late this evening. This will be 
when the main batch of rain begins to initially develop across 
western and central portions of the area. The focus of the 
steadier rain will then shift to the eastern half of the area 
mid-day Friday through the evening hours as the front slowly 
progresses eastward. A wave of low pressure now looks to also 
develop and track along the frontal boundary, which will create 
locally enhanced areas of rainfall. Models continue to wobble 
this corridor of heavier rainfall maximums back and forth a bit,
but the general consensus is for it to be from around Emporia 
through the Middle Peninsula and eastern Northern Neck, up to 
the Maryland Eastern Shore. Its becoming increasingly likely 
that there will be pockets of over 2 to 2.5 inches somewhere in 
that corridor. This will be a favorable environment for locally 
heavy rainfall, with PWATs forecast to increase to 200+ percent 
of normal for early November. In addition, guidance suggests a 
corridor of enhanced mid-level frontogenesis and strong ascent 
associated with the frontal boundary and the developing wave of 
low pressure. This could support a southwest to northeast 
oriented band of moderate to locally heavy rainfall, potentially
persisting over some locations for several hours. Further 
inland, rainfall amounts of 0.50 to 1.00 appear reasonable, with
the lowest amounts expected across our northwestern counties. 
Confidence in those totals of 1.25 to 2 inches across eastern 
VA, northeastern NC, and the Eastern Shore is higher with this 
forecast package, along with the aforementioned pockets of 
higher amounts. 

A few embedded thunderstorms will also be possible Friday, 
particularly across SE VA and NE NC. Forecast soundings indicate
increasing deep-layer shear, generally 30 to 40 kts, with 
modest surface based instability developing in the warm sector 
(~500 J/kg MLCAPE). While the environment could support a few 
stronger storms, widespread cloud cover and ongoing 
precipitation will likely substantially limit destabilization. 
As a result, organized severe weather is generally not 
anticipated, though an isolated damaging wind gust cannot be 
completely ruled out across far SE portions of the area. SPC 
does have a Marginal Risk of severe weather for SE VA/NE NC. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drying out and becoming seasonably cool this 
weekend into early next week. 

The rain will gradually diminish from west to east later Friday
afternoon into Friday night as the cold front pushes offshore. 
A closed low pressure will drop into the northern Mid- 
Atlantic/southern New England region on Saturday, reinforcing 
our northwesterly flow. This will allow drier and cooler air to 
fill into the area, dropping high temperatures back to more 
seasonable values. Highs this weekend and into early next week 
will generally be in the mid to upper 60s. Winds will increase 
across the local waters Saturday evening into Sunday, so some 
coastal locations could see breezy winds. Overnight lows will 
drop into the mid to upper 30s (low 40s by the coast) each 
night. Current model runs are now showing the dry weather 
persisting into the middle of next week as opposed to bringing 
in any more rain chances.
